19660-man-of-many-minds:
E. Everett Evans wrote science fiction for the pulp magazines of the mid-twentieth century. Man of Many Minds is one of his space adventure novels. Its hero, Hanlon, stands before a feared commandant in the opening pages. He fights to hold the man's gaze and mostly fails. The desk between them bristles with communicator studs and plates.

Evans built his stories on fast action and strange mental powers. The title promises a hero whose mind is his main weapon. Pulp readers wanted danger, gadgets, and a tense standoff on page one. Evans delivers that in the first scene. The novel is a sample of the era's brisk, idea-driven space opera.
19882-itinerary-through-corsica-by-its-r:
An Itinerary Through Corsica maps the island by rail, carriage, and forest roads. Edward Lear traveled Corsica and kept a journal of the tour. The guide tradition behind it covers baths, passes, and the Riviera too. Corsica itself is the draw: mountains, forests, and Napoleon's birthplace. Roads there were few, so routes mattered greatly. An itinerary told travelers exactly where each day ended.

Lear, famous for nonsense verse, was also a serious landscape artist. His Corsican journal mixes routes with scenery and incident. Forest roads led him to the island's great pines. Such books served the new independent traveler. They replaced the courier with print. This one preserves Corsica before mass tourism arrived.
20283-women-s-wild-oats-essays-on-the-re:
Women's Wild Oats, from 1920, holds essays on the re-fixing of moral standards. One writer recalls an hour of anxious tension shared by all present. In that hour, each person seemed freed from self in a strange way. Losing individuality, they shared one universal impulse around them.

The colossal importance of that hour made itself felt to everyone. Essays here ask what rules should govern women after the war years. Suffrage, work, and freedom all pressed on old moral codes then. Readers get a sharp set of postwar essays on women and change.
20291-captain-mansana-mother-s-hands:
Captain Mansana and Mother's Hands are two tales first printed in Denmark. Captain Mansana first ran in a Danish Christmas annual, Hill and Dale. That annual was edited by a friend of the writer himself. The tale then ran through two editions in German translation.

Many friends urged the author to reissue it in his own tongue. Now it appears in separate form, paired with Mother's Hands. Scandinavian tales in English dress won many readers in that era. Readers get two tender northern stories in one small, warm volume. Both tales turn on love, duty, and the quiet strength of ordinary folk.
20341-grace-harlowe-s-overland-riders-in:
Jessie Graham Flower wrote Grace Harlowe's Overland Riders in the Great North Woods. A bear under the table throws Grace's companions into sheer panic. Nora puts her foot in a platter of venison in the scramble. The guide explains that Henry, the bear, is a watch dog.

Hippy and the bear meet in hand-to-hand conflict in the fun. Grace Harlowe leads her friends on outdoor trips in this long series. North woods camps bring bears, guides, and tall tales in plenty. Readers get schoolgirl adventure with a comic, woodsy flavor throughout.
20547-stories-of-birds:
Lenore Elizabeth Mulets wrote Stories of Birds, published in 1903, to teach children the birds around them. The stories speak directly to young readers, often as if the child were talking with the bird itself. Field marks come woven into the talk.

I should have remembered your black head and throat, the child says to a chickadee. The sides of your head and neck are white, your breast and sides are light yellow. Your tail and wings are a much darker shade, daintily edged with white. Children learned to name birds by such close, friendly looking.
20560-letters-to-his-friends:
Letters to His Friends preserves the correspondence of Forbes Robinson, with a memoir of his life set before the letters. Robinson was born on November 13, 1867, in the vicarage of Keynsham, a Somerset village between Bristol and Bath. He was the eleventh child in a family of thirteen.

Eight of the children were sons and five were daughters. Their parents raised them in the close world of a country parsonage. Robinson grew into a Cambridge don and chaplain whose letters moved many readers. Friends published them after his early death, as a record of a bright, devoted life.
20561-little-ferns-for-fanny-s-little-fr:
Fanny Fern, one of America's best-loved newspaper writers, made Little Ferns for Fanny's Little Friends for the children who read her columns. The book gathers short stories and sketches sized for young hands. Fern speaks to her readers directly, as she did in print each week.

She tells the children she has some stories she hopes will please and divert them. She would rather have come and told them in person, she says, so she could see their bright faces. Since that could not be, she sends her little book instead. The warmth of that address fills every page.
20576-two-suffolk-friends:
Francis Hindes Groome wrote Two Suffolk Friends as a joint life of two East Anglian clergyman-scholars he admired. Groome is remembered for his work on Gypsy lore. Here he turns to quieter lives: Cambridge men who settled into Suffolk parishes and studies.

One friend passed to Caius College, Cambridge, and took his degree there. In 1833 he was ordained to the Suffolk curacy of Tannington-with-Brandish. Two years later he traveled through Germany as tutor to Rafael Mendizabal, son of the Spanish ambassador. Groome follows both friends through books, parishes, and friendships, in fond and learned detail.
20650-left-end-edwards:
Ralph Henry Barbour's Left-End Edwards is a school football novel, one of his many stories of prep school sport. Edwards plays left end, the position of the title. The book follows his season: practice, rivals, injuries, and the big game that settles the year.

Edwards muses over a pamphlet he has been reading. He does not know, he says to himself with a chuckle. It is something about your mind and your body, though — never mind. He flutters the leaves and glances into the street for friends. Barbour's school tales taught a generation of boys the codes of fair play and team honor.
20669-the-oahu-college-at-the-sandwich-i: The Oahu College at the Sandwich Islands records the founding and charter of the college at Honolulu, in what is now Hawaii. Sandwich Islands was the name Captain Cook gave the Hawaiian chain. The document prints the act of incorporation and the corporation's rules. One article guards its future: trustees must fill any vacancy with all reasonable speed.
21055-a-mating-in-the-wilds:
Ottwell Binns wrote this wilderness novel, published in New York by Alfred A. Knopf in 1920 as part of the Borzoi Western Stories line. It opens on a wide northern river, where a lean, grey-flecked young man paddles steadily toward his goal. Chapters promise a lost girl, a forest fire, and a brave rescue.

Around the paddler the story builds attacks at midnight, a wreck, mysterious shots, and strangers at a tent door. Names like Chigmok and Ainley carry much of the later action, told in separate accounts near the end. Readers get a fast tale of canoes, camps, and danger in the wilds.
21138-love-s-meinie-three-lectures-on-gr:
John Ruskin's three lectures on birds grew from a book begun at Brantwood in 1881, when June snow whitened the Lake District hills around him. He had planned four Oxford lectures holding the cream of forty volumes of bird science. In the end three lectures appeared: on the robin, the swallow, and the dabchicks.

Ruskin explains in a note that meinie is an old English word for a company of attendants. His birds form such a company around the reader. Close watching of feathers, flight, and habit mixes with Ruskin's wide-ranging prose. An appendix rounds out the third edition of 1897.
21300-cowboy-songs-and-other-frontier-ba:
John A. Lomax of the University of Texas collected these cowboy songs and frontier ballads as a Harvard Sheldon Fellow investigating American ballads. First published in 1910 and enlarged in 1916, the book is dedicated to Theodore Roosevelt, who encouraged the work while president. An introduction by Barrett Wendell makes the scholarly case.

Songs of the herd, the stampede, the trail, and the cowboy's death fill the pages, many with music. Lomax gathered them from working cowmen before the open range vanished. He argued the ballads held value for students of western history as well as literature. The collection helped start American folk song collecting as a serious field.
21600-the-flourishing-of-romance-and-the:
George Saintsbury edits and writes The Flourishing of Romance and the Rise of Allegory, on the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The book is the second volume of his Periods of European Literature. Matthew Arnold's line fronts the series: Europe is one great league for mind and spirit.

Saintsbury faced a plain problem: few scholars know all branches of old European writing equally. The volume surveys romance and allegory across many tongues in that rich age. W. P. Ker's Dark Ages precedes it, and F. J. Snell's Fourteenth Century follows. The set ran to twelve crown volumes at five shillings each.
21607-adrift-in-the-ice-fields:
Captain Charles W. Hall sets Adrift in the Ice-Fields among the sea ice of the Maritime Provinces in 1877. The preface promises the youth of America a taste of their neighbours' winter sports. Hall claims no great moral lesson, only true sport and true peril.

A party of English gentlemen shoots sea fowl on the ice in early spring. Hall studied the habits of each bird and beast, and the modes of their capture, with care. The land between the Straits of Canso and Hudson's Bay held leagues no white foot had trod. Drifting ice turns sport to survival in this brisk tale.
21735-the-floating-light-of-the-goodwin-:
Lightships, the floating lighthouses that guard England's worst shoals, stand at the center of this Ballantyne tale. In his preface, Ballantyne says the story shows the work and worth of these vessels and the men who crewed them. He spent a week aboard the Gull-stream light-vessel to learn the life firsthand. Trinity House officers gave him papers, books, and free run of their boats.

The Goodwin Sands, off the Kent coast, were feared by every sailor who passed them. Storms, wrecks, and long dull watches fill the chapters. Ballantyne turns a plain public service into sea adventure. Readers finish knowing why those anchored lights mattered, and what they cost the men who kept them burning.
21760-the-wonder-island-boys-adventures-:
Two boys and a grown man, cast away on a South Sea island with nothing but the clothes they wore, anchor Roger T. Finlay's Wonder Island Boys series. By hard work and cleverness they make clothing, tools, and weapons from what the island gives them. They harness natural forces, tame wild country, and in time win over the fierce tribes nearby.

Adventures on Strange Islands is one volume in the series, each book complete in itself. The boys prepare a vessel, weigh the claims of other islands, and study the customs of the peoples they meet. The publishers promised two thousand useful facts in the series. It is castaway adventure built to teach while it thrills.
21810-the-wonder-island-boys-treasures-o:
Treasure hunting drives this volume of Roger T. Finlay's Wonder Island Boys, a series about two boys and a man cast away in the South Seas. They landed with nothing but their clothes and built a new life by cleverness: tools, weapons, clothing, and command of the island's forces. Earlier books covered the caverns, the tribesmen, and a long capture and pursuit.

Here the boys listen to enemy signals, weigh signs of more than one tribe, and study old sacrifices. John and his friends Uraso and Muro carry the action. Each volume stands alone while the series rolls on. The books promised boys two thousand useful facts along with the adventure, and this one keeps the bargain.
21815-john-forster-by-one-of-his-friends:
John Forster, the friend and biographer of Dickens, gets his own short life here, written by one of his friends in 1903. Forster rose from a struggling newspaperman to chambers in Lincoln's Inn Fields, then to a mansion he built at Palace Gate, Kensington. His fine library room spoke of lettered ease. The writer calls him a man of letters of the old school.

Like Doctor Johnson, Forster led every talk he joined and scorned what he called humbug. He could be rough, despotic, and loud, yet soft-voiced with ladies and people of rank. Beneath it stood deep reading and a fine critical mind. This memoir keeps a strong Victorian personality on record, faults and force together.
21867-afterwards:
Two captives wait for a dawn that means death in the prologue of Afterwards, a desert romance by Kathlyn Rhodes. Dr. Anstice tells Miss Ryder they have only an hour before sunrise. She refuses false hope with a quiet that unnerves him. Nothing on earth, she says, can save them now, and in his heart he knows she is right.

Rhodes had written other desert tales, The Desert Dreamers and The Lure of the Desert among them. This novel flashes back from that hut at night to the road that brought them there. Old talk of a missed picnic and a visit to a temple hints at how long their absence went unnoticed. It is tense, romantic melodrama of the British desert school, built around one long night.
22223-english-songs-and-ballads:
T. W. H. Crosland compiled English Songs and Ballads for the World's Classics series in 1902. Crosland warns readers in his note that the book must not be regarded as a choice. It is simply a gathering, not a best-of. The contents run from old ballads to the drawing-room songs of the nineteenth century.

"Blow, blow, thou winter wind" stands near "Break, break, break" and the bonny brides of Scots song. Love, war, the sea, and parting fill the pages in the national manner. Cheap classics like this one put a small library of song into a coat pocket. The volume shows what Edwardians sang and quoted when they thought of English verse.
22287-smiles-a-rose-of-the-cumberlands:
Eliot H. Robinson published "Smiles": A Rose of the Cumberlands in 1919, and the public demanded more. The title page of later copies lists impression after impression: first in May 1919, tenth by August 1921. Smiles is a girl of the Kentucky Cumberland mountains. Robinson sends her among the feuds, schools, and mission workers of the hill country.

Her nickname is her character: a sunny nature set against mountain poverty and pride. A sequel, Smiling Pass, continued her career by popular request. Such Cumberland romances were a thriving kind, trading on the region's romance for lowland readers. Robinson's rose was among the most reprinted of them all.
22667-joan-of-arc-of-the-north-woods:
Holman Day wrote Joan of Arc of the North Woods, a 1922 novel of the Maine timber country. Day knew the woods and the lumber business from years as a Maine reporter, and his novels pit camp bosses, land men, and settlers against each other among the spruce.

The sample follows Latisan, a timber cruiser, down a tote road from Holeb Mountain after a week alone on the Walpole tract. He has been blazing trees for the choppers and marking twitch roads and yards. A short ax rides in his belt and calipers in one hand. With the other he feeds himself raisins from his pocket. That workmanlike portrait opens a tale whose title promises a heroine raised to lead in the woods war. Day delivers rough country and rough dealing in plenty.
22771-cattle-and-their-diseases-embracin:
Cattle and Their Diseases is a farmer's veterinary manual covering the history and breeds of cattle and the treatment of their ailments. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Before professional vets reached most farms, such a book was the stockman's doctor, consulted at the barn door.

The author had already published The Horse and His Diseases, and the public's warm reception of that book encouraged a matching volume on cattle. The spirit and general treatment are the same: breeds and their qualities first, then symptoms and remedies in plain order. Distempers, fevers, and the management of dairy and beef herds fill the pages. The manual shows nineteenth-century farming knowledge at its most practical, and its limits, on every page.
22882-image-of-the-gods:
Winter closes in on a strange settlement in Image of the Gods. The Dusties have built little furnaces to help fight the cold. What remains is tarring the fields, then buckling down beneath wind shields before the first winter storms strike. Survival here is plain, hard work.

The odd names hint at a world built from scratch, settlers facing an alien season with homemade tools. Science fiction of this kind lives on such practical detail, roofs, fuel, and weather treated as plot. The gods of the title hang over the labor, a question of what these people worship or have made. Readers get atmosphere first and answers later, in the classic magazine manner.
23031-wonderful-adventures-of-mrs-seacol:
Mary Seacole earns a famous tribute in the preface to Wonderful Adventures of Mrs. Seacole in Many Lands. She is the first, the writer says, who redeemed the name of sutler from suspicion of worthlessness and plunder. England, the writer trusts, will remember a woman who tended its sick, hunted up its wounded men to help them, and buried its famous dead.

Seacole's own narrative follows, from Jamaica to Panama to the Crimea. Denied an official post, she built her own British Hotel near the front and fed, doctored, and mothered an army. Her voice is brisk, funny, and proud. The memoir, published in 1857, remains one of the great personal documents of the Crimean War, and of Victorian travel.
23165-the-man-who-stole-a-meeting-house-:
J. T. Trowbridge sketches an unforgettable figure in The Man Who Stole a Meeting-House, dated 1878, from Coupon Bonds. Jedwort leans on a gatepost one particular morning, and the narrator never forgets the sight. The gate itself is too rickety to lean on. Jedwort is a grown man built like a hill, short-legged and stooping. His back swells under his shirt like a sack of grain, and the narrator never forgets the figure he cuts.

A man who steals a whole meeting-house needs building up, and Trowbridge builds him from the gatepost out. His Coupon Bonds tales deal in New England rogues and the neighbors who study them. The theft, a matter of debt, timber, and nerve, unfolds as village legend. Readers get regional humor of the first rank.
23295-grace-darling-heroine-of-the-farne:
Eva Hope's Grace Darling, Heroine of the Farne Islands tells the life of a famous lighthouse keeper's daughter. It opens with a question much argued in Hope's day: what is woman's work? Forefathers, she notes, settled that question more rapidly than her own age could.

In the long ago, she argues, women were less ambitious than in her time. Against that debate, Grace Darling's story stands as evidence. Readers get the tale of a young woman whose courage at sea made her a national heroine. Her story is told by a writer well aware of what that example proved.
338-old-indian-legends:
Zitkala-Sa, a Yankton Sioux writer, retells Dakota legends for children and adults. Old Indian Legends opens with Iktomi the spider fairy, in brown deerskin leggings and beaded moccasins. His painted face and red-banded braids mark him as a trickster.

Iktomi meets ducks, muskrats, coyotes, and fawns, and always learns too late. The badger and the bear, the tree-bound red eagle, and Iya the camp-eater follow. Zitkala-Sa's English keeps the tales' humor and warning. The collection preserves Dakota storytelling in print. Zitkala-Sa later fought for Native rights in Washington.
413-ballads:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers narrative poems of far seas and old wars in this 1895 volume. The Song of Rahero tells a Tahitian legend of slaying and revenge, with notes on island custom. The Feast of Famine treats Marquesan rites, while Ticonderoga follows a Highland name across the Atlantic to war.

Shorter pieces include Heather Ale, a Galloway legend of a secret brew, and Christmas at Sea, a sailor's bleak holiday. Stevenson writes in strong, rolling verse, keen on place and fate. The book shows his gift for tale-telling in meter, from Pacific isles to Scots glens.
438-underwoods:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers verse in English and Scots in this volume, first shaped in the 1880s. Book one holds songs of the road, the sea, and friends, including the famed Requiem with its wide and starry sky. Later books turn to Scots speech, doctors, and the sickroom, with a dedication praising physicians as a rule.

Stevenson stole his title from Ben Jonson and owned the theft with a jest. His lines mix cheer, grief, and a traveler's restlessness. The book shows a poet of wide range, at home in both tongues, and it keeps his most quoted short poems in one place.
922-sunday-under-three-heads:
Charles Dickens wrote this short work on Sunday, dedicated to the Bishop of London. He takes Sunday under three heads, asking how the day should be kept, and for whom. His target is the strict Sabbatarian view that would shut the poor out of innocent recreation, while the rich enjoy their own Sundays in private.

Dickens argues with humour and humanity for a Sunday that allows rest, fresh air, and simple pleasures to working folk. The pamphlet shows his early social conscience and his gift for pleading a cause in plain prose. It remains a lively piece of Victorian debate, on a question that still divides opinion.
931-the-bab-ballads:
W. S. Gilbert wrote these comic ballads under the pen name Bab, for the magazine Fun and later collections. Sailors, policemen, ghosts, and lovers tumble through topsy-turvy plots, told in brisk rhyme with a logic that turns sense on its head. The 1920 Macmillan edition gathers the set for a new generation.

Gilbert's humour is dry, precise, and absurd, and the ballads were the seed of his Savoy operas with Sullivan. Many types and jokes from the stage first appear here, in verse. The book is a treat for lovers of nonsense with a sharp edge, where rhyme and reason play a merry game.
933-more-bab-ballads:
W. S. Gilbert gathered more of his Bab Ballads in this companion volume, with tales such as The Bumboat Woman's Story, The Two Ogres, Little Oliver, Mister William, and Pasha Bailey Ben. Lieutenant-Colonel Flare and other comic heroes follow, each caught in a plot where logic leads straight to folly.

Gilbert's verse is brisk and witty, with rhymes that snap and morals that wink. The ballads show the same topsy-turvy world as the first set, where rank, love, and law are turned upside down. The volume is a further feast for Gilbert fans, and a fine sample of Victorian comic verse at its most ingenious.
a-book-of-golden-deeds:
A Book of Golden Deeds, published in 1864 by Charlotte M Yonge, gathers true tales of brave and selfless acts. Yonge was a popular Victorian novelist and writer for young readers. Rather than inventing a story, she collected real deeds of heroism from history and retold them in short, clear accounts meant to be remembered.

Each tale shows someone choosing courage, loyalty, or sacrifice at a hard moment, often at risk to their own life. Together the stories form a kind of moral gallery, offered to readers as examples worth copying. The book was a Victorian favorite for family and school reading, and it shows how the age taught character through story.
a-bundle-of-ballads:
Henry Morley edited this gathering of old English ballads, with an introduction on the minstrels who once carried such songs from house to house. The contents open with Chevy Chase in two versions, then The Nut-Brown Maid and the outlaw tale of Adam Bell, Clym of the Clough, and William of Cloudeslie. A glossary closes the book.

Robin Hood rides here, with Sir Patrick Spens, Edward Edward, Barbara Allen's Cruelty, The Children in the Wood, and Casabianca. Morley, a tireless editor of cheap classics for working readers, chose ballads for story and singability alike. The volume is a pocket library of the people's poetry, from border raids to ghostly lovers.
a-collection-of-ballads:
Andrew Lang edited this gathering of old English and Scottish ballads, first published in 1897 and reprinted in 1910, with an introduction and notes. The contents open with Sir Patrick Spens, the Battle of Otterbourne, Tam Lin, and Thomas the Rhymer. Many of the songs are centuries old and were carried by singing rather than by print.

The ballads tell of sea wrecks, border raids, fairies, ghosts, true love, murder, and betrayal, in short stanzas made to be sung. Names like Kinmont Willie, Johnnie Armstrong, and the Twa Sisters fill the list. Lang chose well-loved versions, so the book works as a first shelf of the folk ballad tradition.
allan-and-the-ice-gods:
Allan and the Ice Gods, published in 1927 by H Rider Haggard, is the final volume of the Allan Quatermain saga. It forms the fourth part of a loosely linked series that began with Allan and the Holy Flower. Quatermain, Haggard's famous hunter hero, once more takes the hallucinogenic taduki drug, as he did in earlier novels of the series.

Under the drug, he finds himself reliving a past life as Wi, a civilized man living in the barbaric ice age as part of a clan of cavemen. The device lets Haggard set a modern mind inside a prehistoric struggle for survival. The book closes the Quatermain sequence with its strangest journey, into deep time rather than across Africa.
an-unprotected-female-at-the-pyramids:
Anthony Trollope tells a tale of Egypt from the 1864 Chapman and Hall collection Tales of All Countries. He begins by remembering how Grand Cairo filled his young imagination from the Arabian Nights: fantastic houses, beautiful or cunning women, and good-natured, capricious monarchs. The grown traveler finds a different Egypt, full of tourists.

Among them is an English lady traveling without protector or chaperone, determined to see the Pyramids on her own terms. Guides, dragomans, fellow tourists, and a persistent admirer test her independence at every step. Trollope, who knew the tourist world well, mixes satire of travelers' pretensions with real sympathy for his heroine's nerve.
ballads:
Robert Louis Stevenson's Ballads, in its second edition of 1895, gathers his long narrative poems drawn from Pacific and Scottish legend. The Song of Rahero tells a Tahitian tale of slaying and vengeance, with Stevenson's own notes attached. The Feast of Famine does the same for Marquesan manners.

Ticonderoga retells a West Highland legend about a name that brings doom, and Heather Ale recalls the last makers of the Picts' secret drink. Stevenson wrote these poems during his South Seas years, testing whether ballad meter could carry foreign folklore without flattening it. The notes show how carefully he learned the stories from island tellers and Highland tradition.
barrack-room-ballads:
Rudyard Kipling's barrack-room verse fills two series here, the first of 1892 and the second of 1896, forty songs and ballads in all. The dedication is to Thomas Atkins, the ordinary British soldier, in the person of T. A. The contents list the famous names: Danny Deever, Tommy, Fuzzy-Wuzzy, Gunga Din, and Mandalay.

Kipling writes in the soldier's own barrack slang, cockney dropped aitches and all. The subjects are the private's whole world: hangings and route marches, cholera camps and loot, the Widow at Windsor, and the long sail home in Troopin'. Gentlemen-Rankers gives the ruined officer serving in the ranks his own bitter song. No book of verse did more to put the common soldier's voice into English poetry.
beasts-men-and-gods:
Ferdinand Ossendowski's Beasts, Men and Gods carries an explanatory note vouching for its author, a Polish scientist, whom Dr Albert Shaw called the Robinson Crusoe of the twentieth century. The editor admits the adventures seem too highly colored to be real. Part one, Drawing Lots with Death, follows Ossendowski's flight from Bolshevik Siberia in 1920, through forests, frozen rivers, and Red partisans.

Part two enters Mongolia, where he meets the Baron Ungern, the mad White general who took Urga, and hears prophecies in mysterious Tibet. A young woman's corruption shows him, he writes, what depravity Bolshevism brought into the world. The book was a 1922 sensation; historians still argue over how much Ossendowski embroidered.
berlin-and-sans-souci-or-frederick-the-g:
L. Mühlbach's Berlin and Sans-Souci continues her Frederick the Great romances, following the king from the throne room to his beloved palace of carefree ease. Sans-Souci, the little vineyard palace at Potsdam, gives the book its second capital: there Frederick plays the flute, writes French verse, and gathers philosophers instead of courtiers. Voltaire's residence at court stands at the story's center, friendship curdling into rivalry. Berlin supplies the counterweight of guards, parade, and the king's Spartan discipline.

Mühlbach, whose header here reads Louise Muhlbach, writes the enlightened court as domestic drama. Ministers, generals, mistresses of ceremony, and the king's family circle through receptions, concerts, and campaigns' returns. Readers who finished Frederick the Great and His Court get the reign's second act here, the philosopher-king whose friendships were waged like his wars.
bleek-mantis-friends:
Dorothea Bleek edited The Mantis and His Friends for print in 1924. The tales come from her father Wilhelm Bleek's old notebooks. /Xam storytellers had dictated them in the 1870s at Cape Town.

The trickster Mantis leads a cast of beasts, stars, and spirits. His pranks, lusts, and sorrows shape a whole mythic world here. The tales rank as the richest first record of San oral art. Bleek's team caught the voice of tellers whose world was vanishing. Readers meet Bushman folklore at its source, strange and deeply human throughout. The Mantis himself shifts from fool to maker within a single tale.
cap-n-warren-s-wards:
Joseph C Lincoln's novel Cap'n Warren's Wards appeared in 1911, published in New York by D Appleton and Company. New York lawyer Atwood Graves rides a storm-delayed train to Cape Cod on unwelcome business. His errand concerns Captain Elisha Warren, a retired sea captain living quietly in South Denboro. Warren's dead brother has named him guardian of two children.

Caroline Warren is nearly twenty, and her brother Stephen is a year younger. Neither has ever met their uncle, and both resent the arrangement. Graves explains the will, its trust money, and Warren's right to refuse. The captain must decide where the young people will live and how strictly to rule them. Lincoln builds a warm village comedy about family duty, young pride, and an old sailor learning parenthood late.
catalogue-of-british-columbia-birds:
Catalogue of British Columbia Birds, by Francis Kermode, curator of the Provincial Museum at Victoria, lists every bird proven to occur in the province. Kermode dates his preface August 1904. He aims at completeness and admits failure in advance. The list is incomplete, he says, especially for the northern interior. That country, he is sure, is a valuable field for work. The late John Fannin's 1898 list held three hundred thirty nine species and subspecies. Kermode adds twenty four.

Observers across the province supplied local lists, notes, and specimens. Brooks in the Okanagan, Keen in the Queen Charlotte Islands, and Green at Fairview are thanked by name. The catalogue then proceeds by order and family, from the diving birds and grebes onward. Each entry fixes a species to British Columbia on evidence. Museum science here is a network of country observers, mailing skins and sightings to Victoria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-african-synod:
African Synods were not general councils of the entire church, since none was ever held in North Africa. They were many national or plenary bishop assemblies for the North African church, commonly called African or Carthaginian Synods. They must not be confused with district or provincial assemblies, also very numerous in the separate provinces. Those Roman provinces lay between Sahara and Mediterranean, from Cyrenaica east to the Atlantic west, roughly modern Tripoli, Algeria, and Morocco.

There the church entered history late in the second century and vanished early in the eighth. About the mid-third century, bishops of the three civil provinces formed a single ecclesiastical province. As dioceses multiplied, they grouped into divisions matching political divisions. Diocletian redistricted North Africa into six civil provinces; by the late fourth century the church had adjusted to those lines, yielding six ecclesiastical provinces lasting until the Arab invasion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-breads:
Altar breads are one of the two elements required for the Eucharist. Whether Christ used ordinary table bread cannot be told from the sacred text. In the Western Church the breads were probably round, as catacomb pictures show, and Pope St. Zephyrinus called the altar bread a round crown-like offering. Eastern churches use round or square breads.

For valid consecration the host must use wheaten flour and pure natural water, oven-baked or pressed between heated irons, and uncorrupted. Western bread is unleavened, Eastern bread leavened, except among Maronites and Armenians. The large host usually bears Christ crucified, and the breads took many names as sacrament or sacrifice, including gift and host.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-cards:
Altar cards print the prayers a celebrant should know by heart, standing at the altar's middle and each end. They date only from the sixteenth century, and bishops do not use them, reading all prayers from the Pontifical Canon. At Pius V's Missal revision only the middle card existed, called the Tabella Secretarum. Later the Gospel of St. John joined it on the Gospel side, and the Deus qui humanae substantiae prayer with the Lavabo psalm on the Epistle side for symmetry.

Only during Mass do the cards rest on the altar, the middle one against crucifix or tabernacle, the side ones against candlesticks or altar steps. At other times they are removed or laid face down under the altar cover, and when the Blessed Sacrament is exposed outside Mass they must be removed. Framed cards should match the altar's architecture as far as possible.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beguines-begh:
Beguines and Beghards take names most likely from old Flemish beghen, to pray, not to beg, since neither community was mendicant. Other guesses invoke St Bega of Nivelles or Lambert le Bègue, founder of a Liège cloister for crusaders' widows. From the early twelfth century, women in the Netherlands lived alone, vowless, devoted to prayer and good works. Their numbers swelled in the Crusades' age of desolate women, and about 1200 some grouped their cabins into the first Beguinage.

A Beguine was hardly a nun: she took no vows, could wed and return to the world, and kept her property. If poor, she lived by manual labor or teaching burghers' children, not by alms. They waned with the cloth trade, battered by the Reformation's storm and broken by the French Revolution. Belgian foundations fell from ninety-four to twenty by 1856, with membership about 1,600 that year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brothers-of-o: The Brothers of Our Lady of the Fields, a Canadian congregation founded in 1902 at Saint-Damien de Buckland in the Quebec diocese by Father M. J.-O. Brousseau, train orphans in farm and trade work and in settlement arts. The Sisters of Notre Dame of Perpetual Help, founded likewise by Brousseau in 1892, care for the orphans until age twelve, when the brothers take them over. The mother-house stands at Saint-Damien, Bellechasse County, Lac Vert, and the community now counts six brothers and four novices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-camisards:
The Camisards, likely named for their black work blouse, the camise, worn as a uniform, were French fanatics who terrorized Dauphiné, Vivarais, and above all the Cévennes early in the eighteenth century. Their roots lay in the lingering Albigensian spirit, the apocalyptic preaching of French Calvinists, and Louis XIV's harsh methods of conversion after the Edict of Nantes was revoked in 1685. The murder of the Abbé de Chaila in 1702 opened open war.

Armed bands under Séguier, Laporte, Castanet, Ravenel, and Cavalier fought a guerrilla war until about 1705, when they surrendered or were destroyed, and Cavalier's 1709 attempt to revive the revolt failed. A peace treaty with England in 1711 cut off their support, and on 8 March 1715 Louis XIV proclaimed the sect wholly extinct. Much debate surrounds their prophets, some writers holding that Du Serre trained young recruits in a school of prophecy, while Calvinist writers deny any such school existed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caroline-isla:
East of the Philippines in the Pacific lie the Caroline Islands, some 500 small coral islands. Yap, one of the larger islands, lies 1,200 miles from Manila. Spaniards discovered the group in the sixteenth century and named it for Charles V. Jesuit missionaries John Anthony Cantova and Victor Walter tried the mission in 1731, but Cantova was soon murdered and Walter forced to flee, with two more Jesuits killed later.

After the Jesuits' suppression in 1767, no missionary trace appears for 120 years, until Leo XIII settled a German-Spanish dispute for Spain and Spanish Capuchins arrived in March 1886. The Propaganda set up the mission that May in West and East sections, formerly under the Vicariate of Micronesia. The islanders, of Polynesian race, lived by hunting and fishing without farming. A Jesuit weather station on Yap, begun in 1905, cabled typhoon warnings to Manila twice daily.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communion-und:
Patrick Toner's long entry treats Communion under both kinds, set against Communion under one kind alone. One kind means bread alone or wine alone. Both kinds mean distinct reception under bread and wine together, sub utraque specie. Toner works under three heads: Catholic doctrine and modern discipline, history of disciplinary change, and theological speculation. The priest's Communion under both kinds belongs at least to the sacrifice's integrity, and for some theologians to its essence.

History runs from the first century to the twelfth, when public Communion in East and West ordinarily ran under both kinds. Variations fill the record: sick Communion under bread alone at Alexandria, children's Communion before reason, the Presanctified Mass, and intinction, forbidden at Braga. The Utraquist controversy tested the doctrine, and John chapter six supplied texts for both sides. Speculation closes by weighing whether the chalice adds grace by prolonging the species and fervor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faroe-islands:
The Faroe Islands are a Danish group some four hundred miles west of Norway. Fourteen inhabited islands span about 500 square miles of dark, rocky ground. Sheep graze the flowery pastures, and over 100,000 live outdoors all year-round. Fishing, cattle, and bird-catching feed the 16,000 islanders.

Irish monks found the islands first, and Norsemen settled them soon after. Norway ruled them until 1814, and twenty-three Catholic bishops served there. The Reformation ended Catholic life by the close of the sixteenth century. An unfinished Gothic cathedral at Kirkebö still recalls the Catholic age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gilbert-islan:
The Gilbert Islands form a vicariate apostolic of sixteen low atolls near the Equator, the easternmost link of Micronesia, together with the Ellice and Panapa islands. Its chief atolls include Tapiteuca, Arorai, Apemama, Maiana, Marakei, and Nonouti. A Catholic Encyclopedia article describes a people under nominal British protection but practically self-governing, living chiefly by copra.

The vicariate was erected on 17 July 1897, when the Vicariate of Micronesia was divided, under Mgr. Joseph Leray of the Congregation of the Sacred Heart. Of a population reckoned at thirty to forty thousand, fourteen thousand were Catholics. Twelve churches and fifty-six chapels served them, with nineteen priests and ninety-six parish schools. Twelve orphanages sheltered four hundred children, beside houses of religious men and women.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grand-rapids:
Grand Rapids is a diocese created on 12 May 1882 from Detroit, covering the lower peninsula of Michigan north of Ottawa, Montcalm, Gratiot, and Saginaw, an area of 22,561 square miles. At its creation it held about fifty thousand Catholics served by thirty-four priests. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a diocese that prospered steadily under its first bishop.

Henry Joseph Richter, born at Neuenkirchen in Oldenburg in 1838, was ordained at Rome in 1865. He was consecrated at Grand Rapids in April 1883. Belgian and Dutch colonies, with Irish admixture and later Poles, settled its rural regions. By the article's statistics the diocese counted 133 priests, 91 churches with resident priests, 66 parish schools with 13,545 pupils, and a Catholic population of 126,057.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guilds:
Medieval guilds were voluntary associations for worship, fellowship, and trade, reaching their height among the Teutonic peoples, above all the English. The entry sorts them into four kinds, religious guilds, peace or frith guilds, merchant guilds, and craft guilds, and traces the word itself to an Anglo-Saxon verb meaning to pay.

English evidence runs from Ina's seventh-century laws and the Abbotsbury charter under Canute, with its almsgiving, sick care, burials. Masses, to merchant guilds that guarded town trade monopolies, fined outsiders, watched the quality of goods, and doubled as the town's governing body. Craft guilds, later chapters, and the guilds' slow decline carry a vast survey that opens with Brentano's theory of family origins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-imposition-of:
Laying hands on someone is a symbolic rite meant to pass on a gift, a quality, or an excellence, most often spiritual, or to appoint a person to an office. People have used it for worldly ends as well as sacred ones. It reaches back to patriarchal days.

Jacob gave Ephraim and Manasses blessing and inheritance by laying hands on them, and Moses handed Hebrew leadership to Josue the same way. In the New Testament, the Lord used the rite to bring Jairus's daughter back to life and to heal the sick. Its sacred use shows first when Aaron and his sons were set apart as priests, and when priests placed hands on animals offered in sacrifice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ionian-island:
Seven islands west of Greece, with their islets, make up the Heptanesus of this geography entry. Corfu, Paxos, Leucadia or Santa Maura, Ithaca, Cephalonia, Zante, and Cerigo stretch between 36 and 40 degrees north. Together they cover about 1,095 square miles. Their population is put at 261,930. Most islanders belonged to the Greek Orthodox Church, with 6,615 Latin-rite Catholics, a few thousand Jews, and a small Muslim minority.

Mild and healthy air and mountain land still yielded cotton, wine, oil, and raisins in fair amount. The entry's real weight lies in the islands' tangled past and in Catholic life among an Orthodox majority, from bishops and churches to the Latin minority's standing. Readers get both a map and a short history of a borderland between East and West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-shields:
Soldier and senator James Shields, born at Dungannon, County Tyrone, Ireland, on 12 December 1810, died at Ottumwa, Iowa, on 1 June 1879. After emigrating to America in 1826 he took up law at once, opening practice at Kaskaskia, Illinois, in 1832. Illinois voters sent him to the state legislature in 1836, and he went on to serve as state auditor in 1839 and judge of the state supreme court in 1843. War with Mexico found him commissioner of the general land office.

Commissioned brigadier general by President Polk on 1 July 1846, Shields served with distinction under Taylor, Wool, and Scott. He won a major-general's brevet at Cerro Gordo, where a shot passed through his lung. Severely wounded again at Chapultepec, he mustered out in 1848, then governed Oregon Territory briefly before resigning to sit in the United States Senate for Illinois as a Democrat. His life runs from battlefield to Senate chamber.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julian-edmund:
Julian Edmund Tenison Woods was an English-born Australian priest, scientist, and founder. Born at Southwark in London in 1832, he worked for the Times, tried the Passionists, and taught at Toulon, where he caught a love of geology. In 1854 he sailed with Bishop Willson to Tasmania as a schools assistant and was ordained at Adelaide in 1857.

Given a parish of twenty-two thousand square miles around Penola, Woods founded the Sisters of St. Joseph of the Sacred Heart in 1866 with Mary MacKillop, and the Brothers of the Sacred Heart in 1869. He also preached missions across three colonies for eleven years. He died at Sydney in 1889, honored as priest and naturalist alike.

in-the-carquinez-woods:

jerry-of-the-islands:

john-of-the-woods:

joyce-of-the-north-woods:

Garnett translated much of Russia's literature for English readers. Chekhov's jokes about money and work lighten the family record.
life-in-a-thousand-worlds:
The Reverend W. S. Harris published this imaginative volume in 1905. The Minter Company of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, issued it with illustrations. Harris also wrote Mr. World and Miss Church-Member and other religious books. He dedicated this volume lovingly to his mother.

Illustrations promise a city on the Moon and airships on Saturn. One picture shows a trust monopolizing rain and light on Mars. Another offers the largest telescope in the universe. The book blends Christian teaching with a fantastic tour of other worlds. Harris earlier wrote Modern Fables, Sermons by the Devil, and parables. His mother received none of her sacrifices counted too great, he writes.
life-in-the-backwoods:
Susanna Moodie wrote this sequel to Roughing It in the Bush. John W. Lovell published it in New York. Its chapters open with a journey to the woods over corduroy roads. Indian friends, a house fire, and a logging bee follow.

Moodie sketches from nature, claiming painful experience as her teacher. A wall of fire threatens the family in one chapter. Deer hunts and trips to Stony Lake vary the hardships. The book records settler life in the Canadian backwoods firsthand. Stony Lake feasts and squatters' log huts fill the middle chapters. Disappointed hopes reduce the family's fare to milk, bread, and potatoes.
long-odds:
H. Rider Haggard bases this tale on Allan Quatermain's own telling. The Project Gutenberg text follows its reprint in Allan's Wife. Quatermain told the story during an evening in Yorkshire. His only son's death soon unsettled the old hunter completely.

He vanished into Africa with Sir Henry Curtis and Captain Good. A rumored white people drew them toward the unexplored interior. One letter reached Haggard from a mission on the Tana River. Hardships and hopeful traces filled that last report north of Zanzibar. Three hundred miles north of Zanzibar dates the letter's station. Traces raised hopes of a magnificent, unexampled discovery ahead.
lost-on-the-moon-or-in-quest-of-the-fiel:
Lost on the Moon is a boys' science fiction tale by Roy Rockwood. Its young heroes include Mark and Jack Darrow, who read a strange story in a newspaper. Soon they are preparing for a voyage to the Moon itself. An accident and an enemy's plot delay their launch, but at last they are off.

On the Moon they cross craters, find a petrified city, and seek the field of diamonds. A breakdown leaves them lost and wandering on the empty surface. Rockwood piles wonder on wonder, in the manner of early space tales. The book comes from the years before real rockets flew. It offers young readers big dreams and bold adventure.
moby-multiple-language-lists-of-common-w:
Grady Ward granted this language collection to the public domain in January 2001. Moby Language II packages common-word lists in five languages. The files cover French, German, Italian, Japanese, and Spanish, each in plain ASCII text. A historical note says Ward's lists were among the largest public domain word lists in the world when Project Gutenberg added them in 2007.

The lists avoid accented characters and Unicode entirely. Instead, phonetic spellings use backslashes and other marks where accents would fall. The note admits no detailed guide survives for those marks. Translators and programmers still used the files as raw material for language software.
more-bab-ballads:
W. S. Gilbert's second set of Bab Ballads appears here from the 1920 Macmillan edition. The contents list more than forty comic poems. They open with The Bumboat Woman's Story and The Two Ogres. Pasha Bailey Ben, Lieutenant-Colonel Flare, and Lost Mr. Blake follow in Gilbert's flawless rhymes.

Later ballads offer The Captain and the Mermaids, The Fairy Curate, and The Reverend Simon Magus. A long closing piece is simply called Etiquette. Gilbert punctures pompous officials and impossible lovers with an arch, humane voice. These verses, many first printed in the magazine Fun, fed the plots and patter of his famous operas with Sullivan.
more-bywords:
Charlotte M. Yonge gathers nine stories in this companion to her earlier Bywords. The titles mix history and fancy: The Price of Blood, The Cat of Cat Copse, and Sigbert's Guerdon. The Beggar's Legacy, A Review of the Nieces, and Mrs. Batseyes sound a lighter note. A final story is called simply Chops.

The Price of Blood opens in early Christian Gaul, at a town under the needle hills of Auvergne. Processions chant litanies over the cornlands at Rogationtide, a custom newly begun. The crowd mixes Roman, Keltic, Moorish, and Gaelic faces. Yonge uses such scenes to teach church history through story, her lifelong method.
mozart-the-man-and-the-artist-as-reveale: Friedrich Kerst compiled this portrait of Mozart from the composer's own words, and Henry Edward Krehbiel translated it into English. Its title promises the man and the artist revealed without a biographer's middleman. The hosted sample, however, preserves no readable content from the book itself. It contains only the Project Gutenberg header, naming the title, Kerst, and Krehbiel. Readers therefore get the volume's identity and method, Mozart speaking for himself, but the sample offers none of his letters or sayings.
nasa-tm-19630003041-interference-effects:
Beverly Z. Henry, Jr. of Langley wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-218, in January 1960. It studies jets that exhaust from the step of a seaplane hull. The model was of a large, water-based airplane. Tests ran at speeds near the speed of sound.

Henry's summary says two sonic jets were fired through the hull step. Speeds ran from Mach 0.6 to 1.10, at small angles of attack. Fake jets came from hydrogen peroxide units. Lift, drag, and pitching forces were measured, plus hull pressures. The jets' effects on flight forces were checked across that whole range. Such checks kept jet seaplane designs honest.
nasa-tm-19660021047-a-system-for-orienti:
S M Derdeyn and D A Kniffen at Goddard described a cheap system in March 1966 for aiming a balloon payload at one fixed point in the sky. The heart of the system is a sun seeker. Programmed motion corrects for Earth's rotation and for the balloon's drift with the wind. Together, those corrections hold a detector on its target for hours.

Two successful balloon flights had already used the platform when they wrote. Minor changes could adapt it to other jobs. A balloon payload that can stare at one star gathers far more light than one that wanders. Their system gave small research teams that power without the cost of a satellite.
nasa-tm-19720018467-television-data-disp:
Kennedy Space Center described its Television Data Display System in this document, GP-965, dated January 3, 1972. S Sendler is named in the catalog citation for the report. During a launch, computers process a flood of test and flight data. Crews cannot read raw numbers fast enough to act on them. The TDDS turned processed data into television pictures for the firing room. Launch teams could then follow the vehicle's health at a glance.

The report explains the system's general capabilities first. Separate sections then cover its technical features in turn. Operational use leads the list of topics. Computer processed data from prelaunch tests and launches fed the displays. Such display systems became standard in launch control rooms. The document preserves how Kennedy ran its own in the Apollo era.
natalie-or-a-gem-among-the-sea-weeds:
Natalie, published in 1859 under the name Ferna Vale, is a novel about a girl who loves the sea. The title page calls her a gem among the sea weeds. Vale dedicates the book to Hattie, and the preface hopes readers will take up their cross with meekness. Faith sits close to the story from the start.

The first chapter, The Sea Flower, opens with verses on a childhood home by the shore. Gulls, black rocks, foam, and stormy nights fill those lines. The sea stands for freedom against dull life on land. Readers get a moral tale shaped by coast, verse, and Christian duty.
none-other-gods:
Robert Hugh Benson opens None Other Gods with a dedicatory letter to Jack Kirkby. Kirkby, Benson says, was the best friend of Frank, the man the book is about. Frank left the greater part of his diary to Kirkby. Without Kirkby's help, Benson writes, the book could not have been made.

Kirkby also traced the places Frank passed through on his way. Benson thanks him most for the keen impression of Frank himself that he passed on. Frank seems, by that gift, intimately known to a man who never met him. Benson speaks of strange changes in Frank, under old mystical names like Purgation. A friend's life becomes a study of faith.
northern-california-oregon-and-the-sandw:
Charles Nordhoff wrote Northern California, Oregon, and the Sandwich Islands as a travel account of the Pacific coast and Hawaii. Nordhoff had written an earlier book on California, named on the title page. Transcriber's notes in this copy list Hawaiian words whose spelling has changed since his day.

Those notes give lei for a flower garland, and holoku for a Hawaiian black dress. Place names like Nuuanu Valley and Kealakekua Bay are also corrected. One note fixes his claim about taro fields and how many folk a square mile feeds. The notes show a book rich in island detail, read and checked long after its first printing.
october-vagabonds:
Richard Le Gallienne published this autumn travel book in 1911. It follows a walking trip as summer ends. Chapter titles point to woods, orchards, and country roads. Places named include Dutch Hollow and the Susquehanna River. Two friends share the camp, the meals, and the road.

Le Gallienne writes about birds, apples, roses, and small towns. He praises simple food, open air, and slow travel. Some chapters joke about hotels, statistics, and local taste. The tone stays light, warm, and fond of nature. The book suits readers who like gentle outdoor essays. Short chapters keep the walk feeling fresh from day to day.
old-ballads:
Various singers and writers gave the songs gathered in Old Ballads. John Eyre drew the pictures for this edition. The contents list dozens of well loved British songs. Titles include Annie Laurie, Auld Lang Syne, and Home, Sweet Home. Other songs praise sailors, soldiers, and country life.

Readers find love songs, sea songs, and drinking songs together. Burns appears with My Love Is Like a Red Red Rose. Hearts of Oak and Tom Bowling honor the navy. The book preserves songs once sung in homes and streets. It works as a handy songbook of an older Britain.
old-indian-legends:
Zitkala-Sa retold these Dakota legends for general readers. Most tales feature Iktomi, a spider fairy and trickster. Iktomi wears beaded moccasins and red-banded braids. He loves traps, jokes, and easy gains over honest hunting. Other tales treat bears, eagles, rabbits, and a camp eater.

Iktomi's pride often leads him into trouble. Simpler folk outwit him with plain common sense. The tales teach children while honoring Dakota tradition. Zitkala-Sa writes in clear, lively English prose. The book helped carry Native stories to wide audiences. The list also names the Badger and the Bear tale. A dance in a buffalo skull joins the odd set.
old-testament-legends:
Montague Rhodes James retold legends from lesser known Bible books. Longmans published the book in London in 1913. James was provost of King's College, Cambridge. Henry Ford drew ten pictures for the volume. The stories come from apocryphal books of the Old Testament.

Tales treat Adam, Abraham, Job, and Solomon. Readers meet Aseneth, Joseph's wife, in a long story. Solomon commands demons who help build his works. Ahikar outwits the king of Egypt at the end. James writes clearly for general readers and children. The book opens old stories many readers never meet.
on-the-study-of-words:
Richard Chenevix Trench wrote these lectures on English words. The twentieth edition was revised by A. L. Mayhew. Mayhew's preface is dated August 1888 at Oxford. He says he altered Trench's work as little as possible. New research had corrected many old word origins.

Trench was Archbishop and a leader in English philology. His lectures show history hidden inside ordinary words. Words carry the work, wars, and faith of their users. The editor purged derivations now judged impossible in sound. Footnotes point readers to the newest authorities. They helped invent the popular study of word origins.
podcast-joerogan-8SapgxHBxDs:
A wild claim gets a hearing in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience: that a direct energy weapon sits at the South Pole. Rogan looks into the story without endorsing it, treating it the way his show treats most fringe tales, as a puzzle to turn over out loud.

The talk traces where the claim came from and what its believers say the weapon does. Rogan asks what proof would look like and why Antarctica draws so many secret-base stories. The segment is kept as an archive record of the claim itself, a sample of the legends that gather around the world's most remote place.
psalms-of-the-brethren-rhys-davids:
C. A. F. Rhys Davids followed her Sisters volume with the Psalms of the Brethren in 1913. The Theragatha gathers verses by the Buddha's enlightened elder monks. Her translation completed the pair for the Pali Text Society.

Monks muse on forest solitude, impermanence, and hard-won freedom here. Some recall past lives of luxury or crime before ordination. Others praise the Buddha and the peace of the homeless life. The poems rank among the oldest first-person spiritual poetry anywhere. Rhys Davids supplied notes drawing on the ancient commentaries. Together the Sisters and Brethren preserve early Buddhism's human voices most directly.
psalms-of-the-sisters-rhys-davids:
C. A. F. Rhys Davids translated the Psalms of the Sisters into English in 1909. The Pali Text Society published her version of the Therigatha. The Therigatha collects verses by the Buddha's enlightened elder nuns.

Women sing here of release from grief, drudgery, and desire. Former courtesans, grieving mothers, and queens describe their paths to freedom. The poems were composed some twenty-five centuries ago in India. They form the world's oldest surviving women's religious poetry. Rhys Davids, a leading Pali scholar, first carried them to English readers. Triumph and tenderness mark the ancient verses throughout her translation.
quotes-and-images-from-motley-s-history-:
Quotes and Images from Motley's History of the Netherlands is prepared by David Widger. It pairs extracts from John Lothrop Motley's great history with a list of its pictures. The siege of Antwerp is one. Prince William of Orange is another. The Earl of Leicester and Alexander Farnese appear. So does John of Barneveld. The Hague in 1566, the last year of peace, closes the list.

The extracts run alphabetically through the Dutch revolt against Spain. A good lawyer, one line says, is a bad Christian, and it was a penal offence in the republic to talk of peace or truce. A common hatred united the provinces for a time at least, and Motley's country is one disinherited by nature of its rights.
rab-and-his-friends:
Rab and His Friends, by John Brown, M.D., is the famous dog story told here in a Philadelphia edition of 1890, with illustrations by Hermann Simon and Edmund H. Garrett. In his preface Brown tells how the tale began as a lecture for his uncle, the Reverend Dr. Smith, in Biggar, his native village.

He chose Ailie's story. It had haunted him for years. He seemed to hear Rab whining at the door. He seemed to hear James begging on his deathbed. James wanted the world told what his Ailie was. After many failures he wrote it in one night, between twelve and four, and read it, frightened, to the Biggar folk in the school-house.
randy-and-her-friends: Randy and Her Friends, by Amy Brooks, was published at Boston by Lee and Shepard in 1902, with illustrations by the author. The pages shown are the title page and the publisher's list of her popular stories. Three Randy books are ready in cloth at the list's head. Randy's Summer stands at one dollar. Randy's Winter stands at one dollar. Randy and Her Friends stands at eighty cents net. Each book is beautifully illustrated by the author. Each is for younger readers.
rolf-in-the-woods:
Ernest Thompson Seton tells a woodland tale of the War of 1812 years in this book, set out in a long preface. He aims, he says, to picture the forces that shaped American youth a hundred years before: first good citizens, then heroes of Lake Erie, Plattsburg, and New Orleans. Woodland and peace scouting fill the tale in detail.

Seton names his sources: Theodore Roosevelt's Naval War of 1812 and two histories of Lake Champlain, plus unpublished manuscripts and tales from frontiersmen's children. He also means to picture the real Indian, singing and religious, against the scoffs of those who never knew him. Valour and courtesy, he found, lived on both sides of that war.
rollo-in-the-woods:
Jacob Abbott's Rollo in the Woods forms one of the Rollo Story Books, entered at Boston in 1857 under Phillips, Sampson and Company. A picture shows Rollo on the tree bridge, at page fourteen. The contents hold a single story, Rollo at Play in the Woods, told in six short parts.

The parts run in order: The Setting Out, Bridge-Building, A Visitor, Difficulty, Hearts Wrong, and Hearts Right Again. A family outing into the woods thus carries a small quarrel and its mending, in the manner of Abbott's books for the young. This volume holds that one woods tale alone, where the larger Rollo at Play gathers several stories together.
ruth-fielding-at-snow-camp-or-lost-in-th: Alice B. Emerson wrote Ruth Fielding at Snow Camp, or Lost in the Backwoods. The contents list chapters opening with A Lively Time, A Surprising Appearance, The Newspaper Clipping, and The Mysterious Behavior of Fred Hatfield. The party then goes off for the backwoods and travels by train, in chapters headed Off for the Backwoods, On the Train, and A Runaway in Good Earnest.
salt-water-ballads: John Masefield wrote Salt-Water Ballads, issued in New York in 1915 by Macmillan, with a heading that gives the year 1916. The title page notes that the book was set up and published in September 1913 and reprinted in April 1915. A short note signed J. M., dated June 9, 1913, says some of the book was written in the author's boyhood and all of it in his youth. The book is re-issued, he adds, much as it was when first published nearly eleven years before that note.
secrets-of-the-woods:
William J. Long published this nature book in 1901 as Book Three of his Wood Folk series. Long had begun the series with Ways of Wood Folk and Wilderness Ways. Letters from readers asking for more of the wild life of fields and woods moved him to write again.

Long tells how quiet watching reveals the shy habits of woodland creatures. Noise and haste, he warns, scare off the very life a walker hopes to see. Stillness, soft steps, and sharp ears form his method. Young readers and new nature lovers get gentle lessons in how animals live when no one disturbs them.
small-means-and-great-ends:
Mrs. M. H. Adams edited Small Means and Great Ends, dated 1851, as a yearly book for young readers. A front picture shows the widow's pot of oil. In her preface, Adams says the first and second volumes of the Annual met with warm support. That response, she holds, proves the trial of 1845 a success and the small book a fit gift for the young.

Adams thanks old friends who wrote for the book in the midst of hard duties. More pieces came in than could be printed, and she tells those left out that no slight was meant. Their work stays with the publisher for a later year. The contents then begin with pieces named Small Means and Great Ends, Mary Ellen, and The Dead Child to its Mother.
stray-birds:
Rabindranath Tagore's Stray Birds, printed at New York by the Macmillan Company in 1916, is a book of short poems that Tagore himself translated from Bengali into English. A color frontispiece by Willy Pogany faces the title page, and the book is dedicated to T. Hara of Yokohama.

The poems are brief, numbered flights of thought. The first sees stray birds of summer come to a window to sing and fly away, while autumn leaves fall with a sigh. Others speak of tears keeping the earth's smiles in bloom, of missing the stars by weeping for the sun, and of a blade of grass laughing at the desert. Each piece stands alone like a proverb.
sunday-under-three-heads:
Charles Dickens wrote Sunday Under Three Heads as a pamphlet against strict Sabbatarian laws, here printed in the 1905 Chapman and Hall edition of his works at London. He dedicates it, pointedly, to the Bishop of London, whose speeches against Sunday excursions by the lower classes had helped call the pamphlet forth.

Dickens tells the bishop a plain truth. His station gives him countless chances to add to the comforts of the humble. He need not spend a penny of his princely income. He need only bless their harmless pastimes with his example. A prelate so placed, Dickens argues, cannot know the wants of people whose one free day is fenced by law. The pamphlet pleads for innocent recreation over forced idleness.
the-aran-islands:
John M. Synge opens The Aran Islands with a plain account of the ground he lived on. Three islands lie about thirty miles from Galway, up the center of the bay. Aranmor, the north island, is about nine miles long. Inishmaan, the middle island, is three and a half miles across and nearly round. Inishere, the south island, is a little smaller.

Kilronan, the chief village on Aranmor, has been changed by the fishing trade. That trade was built up by the Congested Districts Board. The village now looks, he says, like any fishing village on Ireland's west coast. The other islands stay more primitive, though change is creeping in there too. Synge promises a straight tale of his life among the islanders, with nothing made up and names disguised.
the-bab-ballads:
W. S. Gilbert's comic verses appear in a Macmillan edition of 1920, reprinted many times since a sixth edition in 1904. Earlier forms include a Routledge edition of Fifty Bab Ballads in 1884. Listed titles range from Captain Reece and The Rival Curates to General John.

Other ballads in the contents include Sir Guy the Crusader, Haunted, and The Bishop and the 'Busman. Ferdinando and Elvira, or The Gentle Pieman, promises a mock tale in verse. The table gives page numbers for each piece, so readers can dip into short, rhymed stories about sailors, clergy, lovers, and fools rather than read straight through.
the-birds:
Aristophanes' comedy, in an uncredited translation with footnotes explaining Greek names, terms, and puns, is introduced as an extravaganza. Unlike his other surviving plays, it has no clear serious political aim under the fun. Bright dialogue, lyrical interludes, stage effects, and fine dresses are its stated attractions.

The play was produced in 414 B.C., while the Sicilian Expedition hung in doubt and Athens still reeled from the mutilation of the Hermae. Some critics read Sicily and Alcibiades into it, the introduction says, but the author seems to be giving anxious citizens relief. It failed to win first prize, losing to a rival play by Amipsias.
the-book-of-old-english-ballads: A Book of Old English Ballads holds old songs with art by George Wharton Edwards and a first word by Hamilton W. Mabie, dated 1896. The list names Chevy Chace, King Cophetua and the Beggar-Maid, and King Leir and his Three Daughters. Fair Rosamond, Phillida and Corydon, and Fair Margaret and Sweet William come next. Annan Water, The Bailiff's Daughter of Islington, and Barbara Allen's Cruelty are there too. The Douglas Tragedy, Young Waters, Flodden Field, and Helen of Kirkconnell follow. Three Robin Hood songs close the list.
the-breitmann-ballads: Charles G. Leland wrote The Breitmann Ballads. The pages shown are Project Gutenberg head matter only, dated March 1996, with no ballad text at all. They name Leland and the book, and note a twin HTML form of the file. A later note says the file was made by Geoffrey Kidd and Krista Rourke of Berkeley, California. It also says the file holds two copies of the ballads, one in plain ASCII and one with HTML marks.
the-call-of-the-cumberlands:
Charles Neville Buck opens The Call of the Cumberlands close to the backbone of the Cumberland ridge. The sun hesitates before its descent. A sugar-loaf cone towers above a creek called Misery, edged with emerald where the tallest timber thrusts into the light. Below, where the waters toss along in tiny cascades, the light thickens into a cathedral gloom. No travelers pass, and no living throat sounds but the bob white of a nesting partridge and the song of a red cardinal among the pines.

Suddenly the leafage is thrust aside from above by a cautious hand. A shy, half-wild girl appears in the opening. She halts, lifts her face, and listens. The partridge calls across the slope, and with perfect imitation she whistles back an answer. She is, the tale says, as much a wood creature as the birds themselves.
the-camp-fire-girls-go-motoring-or-along:
Hildegard G. Frey wrote The Camp Fire Girls Go Motoring, or Along the Road That Leads the Way. A plate shows a girl crying, in a tone of desperation, that she is running away. Chapter I is told by the official reporter of the Winnebagos, at Nyoda's bidding. The story of their automobile trip last September, she says, was too good to keep to themselves.

The whole train of events hinged on a commonplace circumstance: tan khaki outing suits were the fashion of the summer before. The night after the girls came home from Onoway House, the narrator sat at her window watching the stars come out. Longfellow's line on the lovely stars, the forget-me-nots of the angels, set her thinking of Evangeline.
the-clouds:
Aristophanes wrote this comedy, translated here by William James Hickie, with all Greek transliterated into Roman letters. The cast list names Strepsiades, his son Phidippides, Socrates and his disciples, a chorus of Clouds, and the Just Cause and Unjust Cause. The scene is a sleeping apartment at midnight.

Strepsiades sits up in bed and curses the length of the nights. The cock crowed long ago, his servants snore, and war, he complains, keeps him from even punishing them. His fine son sleeps on through the night, wrapped in five blankets, taking his ease. The father cannot sleep for torment over his expenses, his stud of horses, and his debts, all run up through that son. Aristophanes builds the play on that household clash: a father ruined by a horse-mad son, turning toward Socrates and his school for a way out.
the-curious-book-of-birds:
Abbie Farwell Brown wrote The Curious Book of Birds, published in Boston and New York by Houghton, Mifflin and Company in October 1903, with pictures by E. Boyd Smith. Her foreword scolds modern bird books for giving only facts: the singer's house, his habits, his mate's eggs, and the color of each feather.

Such books, she says, tell nothing of bird history, of what birds have meant to people since the world began. The quaint fancies about birds are in danger of being lost, though they show why we like some birds and dislike others and why poets use their nicknames. Facts, she warns, are not what one looks for in a curious book, and any that crept in among the old fancies earn the book's apology to its child readers.
the-deliverance-a-romance-of-the-virgini: Only a Project Gutenberg header stands at the head of this record for The Deliverance, a romance of the Virginia tobacco fields, by Ellen Glasgow. The header dates the electronic text to November 2000, numbers it Etext 2384, and carries the usual notes on copyright and keeping the file. No title page, contents, or chapter text follows in what is present here.
the-eustace-diamonds:
Anthony Trollope's The Eustace Diamonds first ran in the Fortnightly Review from July 1871 to February 1873. Contents open with Lizzie Greystock, then Lady Eustace, Lucy Morris, and Frank Greystock, before The Eustace Necklace names the prize. Later heads track Lord Fawn at his office, the diamonds seen in public, and a claim that the necklace is an heirloom.

Lizzie, a young widow, holds a famed diamond necklace her late husband's kin call theirs. Lies, theft, and two suitors swirl round the gems. Trollope spins a sharp tale of greed and charm.
the-false-gods:
George Horace Lorimer, known for his letters from a self-made merchant, wrote The False Gods as a work of fiction printed by D. Appleton in New York in 1906. Only title pages and picture captions stand at the head of this copy.

One caption shows a man crushed against a stone breast by great arms, a scene of sudden, strange death. That single image hints at the book's blend of city life and eerie peril. Lorimer steps away from his famed merchant letters here and tries a shorter, sharper tale of modern folk and the false powers they bow to.
the-freelands: John Galsworthy wrote The Freelands as a novel, dated 1915 in this copy's heading, and only the front matter and contents are present here. The contents list a prologue and chapters named by number alone, running past eighteen with no heads or hints of scene. No page of the novel itself is included in this portion, so nothing about the Freeland family or its land can be described from the front matter alone.
the-garies-and-their-friends:
Frank J. Webb wrote The Garies and Their Friends in 1857, a novel of free Black life in Philadelphia, given by leave to Lady Noel Byron. The preface states the book's aim in plain terms.

Webb, a young Black man born and raised in Philadelphia, asks if the race held in bondage can bear freedom, self-rule, and growth. His city, on the edge of free and slave land, drew runaways and freed folk who built wealth and standing of their own. The Garie family moves from the South into that world. Webb shows schools, homes, and mobs through the eyes of folk who lived the question.
the-illustrated-alphabet-of-birds:
Young children learned their letters from this picture alphabet, dated 1851 and preserved through the Baldwin Library at the University of Florida. Each letter introduces a bird in a short rhyming verse with its own illustration. A is an auk of the Arctic sea, living on the ice where the winds blow free; B is a blue bird, whose songs ring through the forest in early spring.

The pattern continues through the alphabet, pairing the shape of each capital and small letter with a creature and four lines of verse. Books like this one taught reading, natural history, and rhyme at the same time, in an age when a child's alphabet book was often the first illustrated volume in the house. The scans behind the text come from a copy meant to be handled by small hands.
the-knave-of-diamonds: Ethel M. Dell published this novel in 1912, a year after The Way of an Eagle, dedicating it to her friend and sister. Kipling's verses to the true romance stand as its motto. Only the dedication pages and first contents are present here. The story itself does not appear. Part I opens with The Missing Heart. The Queen's Jester and The Chariot of the Gods follow. Cake Morning, The First Encounter, and At the Meet come next. The Fall, The Ride Home, and The Head of the House close it.
the-life-of-the-fields: Richard Jefferies gathered his nature essays from many magazines, and his thanks page names the editors who first printed them. Only that page and the contents are present here, listing the pageant of summer, the field play, bits of oak bark, meadow thoughts, clematis lane, and nature near Brighton. Pieces also cover Sussex woods in January, the river Exe, and birds climbing the air. The essays themselves are absent from this record beyond those titles.
the-man-from-the-clouds: J. Storer Clouston's The Man from the Clouds is dated 1919. Only the title page and part of the contents are present, so the novel does not appear. Part one chapters shown include In the Clouds, The Man on the Shore, Alone Again, and The Suspicious Stranger. The Doctor's House, At the Mansion House, The Coast Patrol, A Near Thing, and On the Drifter follow. They point to a mystery that begins with a man arriving from the sky. It moves through suspicion on a coast watched for enemies.
the-masters-of-the-peaks-a-story-of-the-: Joseph A. Altsheler published The Masters of the Peaks in 1918, a story of the Great North Woods in his French and Indian War series. Only the title page and the list of characters are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The list names Robert Lennox, a lad of unknown origin, the Onondaga warrior Tayoga, and the hunter David Willet.
