the-patient-observer-and-his-friends: Simeon Strunsky wrote The Patient Observer and His Friends, published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1911. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here, so the essays themselves do not appear. The contents list short pieces named Cowards, The Church Universal, and The Doctors. Interrogation, The Mind Triumphant, and On Calling White Black follow. The Solid Flesh and Some Newspaper Traits complete the list shown, the light essays of a newspaper columnist.
the-pilots-of-pomona-a-story-of-the-orkn: Robert Leighton's The Pilots of Pomona, a story of the Orkney Islands, appears here through its contents alone. Only the chapter list is present, so the story itself does not appear. Forty chapters are named, opening with a boy late for school, his teacher Andrew Drever, and Sandy Ericson, Pilot. Middle entries include the wreck of the Undine, a rescue, and a cave adventure below ground. Late chapters promise a light in the Gaulton Cave, a search, a boy trapped and arrested, and an accusation of murder.
the-place-beyond-the-winds:
Harriet T. Comstock's The Place Beyond the Winds was published by Doubleday, Page and Company at Garden City, New York, in 1914. Harry Spafford Potter drew the illustrations. A list of illustrations quotes lines from the story. One line calls a dance grotesque, pagan, and yet divine. Another has bottles whirling and crashing on rocks near a roadway. A third speaks of a promise kept past the Dreamer's Rock, out to the open sea.

Chapter I introduces Priscilla Glenn standing on the little slope from the farmhouse down to the spring. She lifts her head like a young deer sensing something new or dangerous. The day is a lovely one in May that feels more like June. That is rare for the place called Kenmore, where seasons lapse into one another as calmly as everything else. A change is plainly on its way into her quiet life.
the-problem-of-the-ohio-mounds: Cyrus Thomas's The Problem of the Ohio Mounds is identified in its Project Gutenberg header as Etext 4248, released in July 2003. The header says the file was first posted in December 2001 and prepared by volunteers. Nothing of Thomas's report on the mounds appears in the pages provided: they consist of the old-style Gutenberg header alone, with its copyright cautions and welcome to free electronic texts.
the-reign-of-law-a-tale-of-the-kentucky-:
James Lane Allen dedicates his Kentucky tale to the memory of his father and mother, then opens with a long meditation on hemp. Early Anglo-Saxon farmers, he writes, sowed hemp as soon as they won footholds in the western wilderness, remembering Virginia and Britain.

Allen fixes a date, August 12, 1782, when two riflemen rode from Bryan's Station to rouse settlements while hemp already grew tall by the fort walls. Hemp first served cabin needs for rope, towels, and shirts, then fed shipbuilding and cotton country demand. Place and crop become a lens for Kentucky character and conflict.
the-riddle-of-the-sands: Erskine Childers edits a record of secret service here. The service was lately achieved, the subtitle says. Maps and charts are promised for the voyage. Contents run through a letter first. A yacht named Dulcibella follows. A sailor named Davies joins the account. Fiords, a missing page, and a theory come next. Night work among islands fills the middle chapters. A German commander and a stowaway's luck close the list. A double aim ends the record. Only the title pages and contents list are present here.
the-rover-boys-on-land-and-sea-the-cruso:
Seventh in the Rover Boys series, The Rover Boys on Land and Sea carries the subtitle The Crusoes of the Seven Islands. Arthur M. Winfield wrote the volume. Its introduction says the story is complete in itself. Winfield first meant to write only three volumes about Dick, Tom, and Sam Rover.

The contents carry the boys from San Francisco to Santa Barbara. They board a yacht there, then drift on the Pacific Ocean. Headings promise another castaway brought to light. Sam meets a shark, and a cave is explored. A fight with a wild beast follows. The wreck burns near the end. The final heading promises a defense of the cave, in which the party is saved.
the-school-for-husbands:
An introductory notice precedes The School for Husbands, a comedy in three acts whose original was in verse. The French title is L'École des Maris. The notice says this was the first play whose title used the word school. The word implied a special lesson beyond amusement. Molière meant married men to find instruction and warnings, the notice argues.

The comedy was first played at Paris on June 24, 1661. It met with great success there. On July 12 it was acted at Vaux, Fouquet's country seat, before the whole court. The notice traces its main idea to Terence's Adelphi. Two old men of unlike character raise children differently in that model. A tale from Boccaccio's Decameron is also discussed. The notice calls the play a distinct departure for Molière. Character, not plot machinery, now gives rise to situations.
the-story-of-ida-pfeiffer-and-her-travel:
An unnamed writer tells the life of the celebrated traveller Ida Pfeiffer. Thomas Nelson and Sons published the book in London in 1879. It has four parts. They cover her life and her journey round the world. A northern journey and her last travels follow. Chapter one records that she was born in Vienna on October 14, 1797, the third child and only girl in a family of six, to a well-to-do merchant named Reyer.

The young Ida was bold and enterprising, contemptuous of dolls, fond of drums, swords, and guns, and happy dressing like her brothers. Her father encouraged her tastes. He fed her simply and trained prompt obedience. He died when she was ten. A great contest followed. What she wanted fought against her mother's ideas of how a girl should be raised.
the-tangled-threads: Eleanor H. Porter's Tangled Threads, copyrighted in 1919 and published by the Christian Herald, collects twenty of her short stories. This record shows the title page, the contents, and a note that the stories first appeared in magazines such as Lippincott's, Harper's, and McCall's. Titles include A Delayed Heritage, Crumbs, Millionaire Mike's Thanksgiving, and When Polly Ann Played Santa Claus. The stories themselves do not appear in the pages present, so Porter reaches readers here only as a table of kindly, home-centered subjects.
thoroughbreds:
W. A. Fraser dedicated Thoroughbreds to his wife, calling her a thoroughbred, and set the story in Brookfield, a village less than a hundred miles from Gotham. A century of growth around it has pinched the hamlet into isolation. Horse racing divides its people.

The Reverend Dolman opposes racing, while Honest John Porter treats honest racing as a religion inherited from his Kentucky father. Porter's wife hates the sport, daughter Allison loves horses, and son Alan works among bank figures. Banker Philip Crane secretly races too. Readers get a village novel about sport, faith, and family loyalty.
uncle-wiggily-in-the-woods: Howard R. Garis's Uncle Wiggily in the Woods, copyright 1917 and illustrated by Louis Wisa, belongs to his Bedtime Stories. The contents pair the old rabbit with a tree or plant in nearly every tale: the willow, the wintergreen, the slippery elm, and the sassafras open the list. Later stories bring the violets, the birch, the butternut, and the horse chestnut. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the woodland adventures themselves do not appear.
under-the-redwoods:
Bret Harte gathered ten stories and sketches in Under the Redwoods, most of them rooted in California mining and town life. Titles in the contents include a widow of the Santa Ana Valley, a mermaid at Lighthouse Point, three vagabonds of Trinidad, and a look back at bohemian days in San Francisco. The opening piece, Jimmy's Big Brother from California, begins on a stormy night at a mining settlement called Sawyer's Ledge.

That first story sets two cabins against each other. One glows with many candles for a party honoring Robert Falloner, a miner who has struck luck. The other holds the sickbed of Dick Lasham, a miner whose luck has failed, watched over by his hopeful neighbor Daddy Folsom. Readers get Harte's mix of humor, hardship, and local color, built from short scenes of western life rather than one long plot.
underwoods:
Robert Louis Stevenson published his poems as Underwoods, and the title page here shows the ninth edition, printed in London by Chatto and Windus in 1898. A short verse before the dedication jokes that he stole his title from a better man and wishes he had stolen the whole book. The poems themselves gather work in English and in Scots, much of it tied to his home ground and his years of poor health.

Stevenson aimed his long prose dedication at doctors. He praises physicians as the flower of the age, men of generosity, discretion, and tact, tested by secrets and hard moments. He thanks the few, out of many, who brought him comfort and help in sickrooms. Readers meet the poet first as a grateful patient, and that note of thanks colors the verses that follow.
vane-of-the-timberlands: Harold Bindloss wrote Vane of the Timberlands, a novel of the Canadian woods. Pages shown here hold the title page, a contents list of thirty-one chapters, and the heading of chapter one, so the story itself is not shown. Chapter titles place Vane in Vancouver, on the heights, storm-stayed, and in the bush, and name Lucy Vane, Chisholm, Evelyn, and Jessy, whose favor, blow, and remorse all get chapters. The closing titles promise the end of a search, testimony that convinces, and Vane reinstated.
volcanic-islands:
Charles Darwin's Geological Observations on the Volcanic Islands reports what he saw of island geology on his voyage. An editorial note at the front grants that the books reprinted here are more technical than Darwin's Journal, yet praises the freshness of the observations. Many parts, it says, give a fine way into questions about the structure and changes of the earth's surface, and form a charming start in physical geology.

The contents run from St. Jago in the Cape Verde group through Fernando Noronha, Terceira, and Tahiti, then Ascension, St. Helena, and the Galapagos Archipelago. A late chapter weighs trachyte and basalt and the spread of volcanic isles, and the last turns to Australia, New Zealand, and the Cape of Good Hope. The note adds that the original books cost many times this volume's price. Students get a master mind reasoning on the ground he walked.
what-sami-sings-with-the-birds:
Johanna Spyri wrote What Sami Sings with the Birds, brought into English by Helen B. Dole in 1917. The tale opens by Lake Geneva after three days of spring sun. Rain has stopped, and a soft breeze moves over the blue water. Chapter one bears the name Old Mary Ann.

The contents promise a stay at a grandmother's house, a new life, and hard times. Later the birds still sing, and at last Sami sings too. Spyri, famed for Heidi, tells of a poor boy and the comfort of nature. Gentle faith and alpine scenes shape the short tale. Young readers meet loss softened by song.
with-trapper-jim-in-the-north-woods: Lawrence J. Leslie wrote this 1913 boys' adventure for the Campfire and Trail Series. Pages present here give the title page and chapter list, but no story text. The chapter titles promise woodcraft lessons, trapping secrets, a silver fox chase, and an unwelcome guest smoked out of camp. Two chums and a woodsman named Trapper Jim lead the action, judging by the titles alone.
yule-tide-in-many-lands: Mary P. Pringle and Clara A. Urann wrote this illustrated survey of Christmas customs, published in Boston in 1916. Pages present here hold title pages, a Tennyson motto about old customs yielding to new, and a frontispiece note. That picture shows Christmas in Naples with an Italian crib scene. No chapter text appears in these pages. The survey's country-by-country accounts themselves stay absent, beyond the title's promise of many lands.
